title: Will Stein admits he was conservative on offense in Alabama loss
description: The Cats will aim to move the offense in the right direction when they travel to Texas A&M on Saturday.
fullText:
Kentucky Football fans entered year one of the Will Stein era optimistic and eager to see a new, more exciting brand of football at Kroger Field.

This offseason, the BBN shared a collective sentiment centered heavily on the simple eye test. It's fair to say most UK fans have approached this season with a focus that goes beyond simply tallying wins and losses.

For all the good Mark Stoops did for the Kentucky football program, his offensive approach didn't exactly make for must‑see TV. So the introduction of Will Stein's playbook became one of, if not the, biggest reasons to bring him to Lexington.

The stage was set Saturday when Kentucky hosted Alabama, offering a true benchmark for where this team stood offensively. The results were tough to swallow.

Aside from a few first‑half flashes, Kenny Minchey struggled to generate much under center against the Crimson Tide. Explosive plays were nearly nonexistent, prompting head coach Will Stein to address the lack of offensive production fans are craving.

"We've got to be able to generate and create explosive plays. I think that's obvious," Stein stated during his Tuesday press conference.

Stein went on to explain that he wanted to stay conservative in key moments, but that isn't something he and offensive coordinator Joe Sloan want to do.

"There were specific times in the game that I felt like we could have taken those punches," said Stein about going for more aggressive plays. "And that's not a Joe Sloan problem. That's a me problem. So what can I do as a head coach in those moments to give our players and give our coaches that type of confidence to go out there and swing when we have a chance?"

It's encouraging to see that, even after reflection, the goal remains to put it all on the line and try to win the football game — even against a powerhouse like Alabama.

Stein and his staff won't have to wait long to put that mindset into practice. They'll face one of the toughest challenges in college football this weekend when they travel to No. 9 Texas A&M. It's unfair to make firm assertions with only eight quarters of game film to go on, but there's no denying that another poor showing for the offense this weekend and things could begin to spiral.

Currently, Kentucky is a heavy 16.5-point underdog with only a 6.5% chance of pulling off the upset, according to ESPN.

fullText:
The Knicks have one open roster spot left (that they can afford under the second apron), and it looks like they'll use it on guard depth.

Veteran guard John Konchar has agreed to a one-year deal with the Knicks, a story first reported by Shams Charania of ESPN and since confirmed by Konchar's agents.

Congratulations to @konchjitty55 on signing with the @nyknicks ✍️ pic.twitter.com/RoUjmhj7du

This is likely a non-guaranteed contract, but Konchar had options and would not have signed somewhere he didn't believe he was likely to make the final roster. The Knicks also signed veteran big man Drew Eubanks to a training camp deal, and he is competing for a roster spot, reports the well-connected Ian Begley of SNY.TV.

Konchar is a reliable 6'5" guard who has been in the league for seven years. He plays smart basketball, is a solid rebounder who averaged 4.3 a game last season splitting time between Utah and Memphis, and he is a career 34.9% shooter from 3-point range. That said, he's not much of a scorer (4.3 points per game for his career).

The Knicks have 13 standard contracts on their roster and Konchar brings them to 14 and close to the second apron.

title: Rutgers Shuts Out No. 16 Princeton 2-0 to Close the Homestand
description: Abubakar Mayanja scored before the first of two trips to the bench, William Pierce came on for a center back and beat a ranked opponent's goalkeeper, and Rafael Ponce de Leon made five saves
fullText:
PISCATAWAY, N.J. — Rutgers had conceded a goal in every match it played this season, six games and five different results, the most recent of them Friday's 3-1 win over No. 11 UCLA. On Tuesday, closing a five-game homestand against the best record to visit Yurcak Field all year, the Scarlet Knights finally kept a clean sheet. They beat No. 16 Princeton 2-0 in front of 508, handing the Tigers, 4-0-1 coming in, their first loss of the season.

Both goals came in the first half, 29 minutes apart, from a starting forward who would leave the match and come back twice and a substitute who entered for a center back. Abubakar Mayanja scored in the 11th minute and was subbed off in the 30th. William Pierce, on since the 30th for Hector Criado, doubled the lead in the 40th and was himself pulled just after the hour. Both finishes went into the same corner of Andrew Samuels' net.

Rutgers arrived at 2-3-1 off the best result of its season, the upset of 11th-ranked UCLA that had brought its goal total to eight in six matches: four of them scored in a single night against Sacred Heart, three against the Bruins, one in between. The goals-against column had not moved. Rutgers had allowed a goal in each of its first six games, and Rafael Ponce de Leon carried 18 saves on the year into Tuesday's match without a shutout to show for any of them.

Princeton was unbeaten and ranked 16th nationally entering the match, by record the most accomplished team to visit Rutgers this homestand. None of that showed for the first 45 minutes. The Tigers managed a single shot in the opening half, off their single corner of the opening half, and went into the locker room down two goals to a team they were favored to beat.

D: Devon Stopek, Nick Collins, Hector Criado, Erick Ruiz, Braxton Montgomery

M: Pius Ssebulime, Zach Mastrodimos, Francesco Di Ponzio

F: Thomas Angelone, Abubakar Mayanja

Subs: Simon Gorczowski, William Pierce, Joshua Jerome, Amer Lukovic, Jeffrey Bryjak, Dylan Carlson, Noah Hannawald, Jaeden Gordon

Rutgers made four changes at once in the 30th minute, still up only 1-0 with Gorczowski on for Angelone, Pierce on for Criado, Jerome on for Di Ponzio, Bryjak on for Mayanja. Ten minutes later, one of the four scored, Pierce, beat Samuels off a Ruiz service with Ssebulime credited on the build.

The reshuffling didn't stop there. Three Rutgers starters left the match and came back before the final whistle, Angelone, Di Ponzio and Mayanja each played two separate stretches, and Jerome did the same from the bench, entering in the 30th minute, coming off at halftime, and returning in the 63rd. It was the second match in three days in which Rutgers brought a substituted player back into the game and Tuesday, it happened four times over. By the 63rd minute, three of the four players directly responsible for Rutgers' goals as Mayanja, Pierce and Ruiz were off the field for good, joined by Ssebulime and Montgomery before the 80th.

Princeton countered with its own churn with three substitutions by the 28th minute, four more at halftime, three 

Rutgers won a corner 70 seconds into the match and another 43 seconds after that, with a blocked Mayanja attempt in between, and the shape of the half was set inside two minutes. Princeton spent the opening quarter-hour retreating into restarts, seven throw-ins in the first nine minutes, and did not put a meaningful touch into the Rutgers box until the 35th.

It came in the 11th as Braxton Montgomery moved it forward, Francesco Di Ponzio touched it on, and Mayanja finished left-footed into the bottom left corner. The match then went through a bit of a tactical back and forth. Zach Mastrodimos was awarded two free kicks inside that span, Hector Criado and Erick Ruiz one apiece, and Rutgers kept the ball in the Tigers' half. Mayanja fired over in the 26th, Di Ponzio missed the target in the 29th, and Princeton went to its bench for three changes in the 28th minute, still trailing by one and still without a shot.

The first arrived in the 36th and was also its last of the half. Tsunehara won Princeton's only first-half corner in the 35th and forced Ponce de Leon into a low save to his left a minute later. Two minutes after that, Rutgers put the ball in the Princeton net and did not get to keep it, flagged offside in the 38th. The official play-by-play logs the offside call and nothing else, however my own eyes did not deceive me. Jim McElderry argued the decision at length, and his frustration with it carried through the rest of the match, justified given many of the poor calls by the referred. No caution was shown to the Rutgers bench though.

Pierce settled the half at 39:59

He showed off a right-footed finish into the bottom left corner, the same corner Mayanja had found 29 minutes earlier. Joshua Jerome nearly made it three in the 42nd, forcing the only save Samuels had to make before the break, and Rutgers won its fourth corner a few seconds later. Princeton went to halftime having taken one shot.

Princeton made four changes at the interval with Noah Hammerschmidt, Cyrus Klinenberg, Giacomo Gabrielli and Benjamin Manfroy all on. The reshaped Tigers took the match over territorially without ever taking it over anywhere that counted. Nick Collins put Rutgers' first attempt of the half off target in the 48th and Mastrodimos had one blocked in the 55th. Tsunehara had Princeton's first blocked in the 59th. Then Princeton settled in and Rutgers stopped coming forward.

Between the 66th and the 72nd minute the Tigers won four corners, at 65:46, 68:01, 70:44 and 71:29, and did not manage a shot from any of them, not surprising at all. Pius Ssebulime conceded three fouls across that stretch and the one before it. Rutgers had already pulled Pierce, Mayanja and Ruiz in the 63rd, and by the 79th Ssebulime and Montgomery were gone too, replaced by Dylan Carlson and a returning Thomas Angelone.

Julien Lacher, back on in the 74th after starting the match, produced the best two looks Princeton generated all night. Ponce de Leon saved the first low to his right in the 78th and the second low to his left 42 seconds after that. Lacher had a third blocked in the 82nd and Manfroy had one blocked six seconds later.

The most dangerous Tiger on the field, though, was the one who spent 82 minutes off it.

Ian Nunez entered in the 82nd, took two shots in eight minutes, and put both on frame, and they were saved top left in the 84th and saved bottom center at 89:03, the last touch of consequence in the match. It was probably a blessing that Princeton did not know how to appropriately use him tonight.

Rutgers' only shot on target of the second half belonged to Amer Lukovic, saved by Samuels in the 84th, nine seconds after Nunez's first. Lukovic had picked up the match's only card five minutes before that, a yellow for unsporting behavior in the 80th, which seemed . Rutgers won one corner after halftime, in the 84th, and took four shots to Princeton's seven. The Tigers finished with 14 fouls to Rutgers' 10, six second-half corners to one, and the same number of goals they had at kickoff.

Rutgers moves to 3-3-1 and takes their first shutout of the season on the road, first to Ohio State on Sept. 18 and then to defending national champion Washington on Sept. 25. Ponce de Leon is now at 23 saves against six goals allowed through seven matches, five of those saves, and none of the goals, coming Tuesday, against three different Princeton shooters.

For the second time in, Rutgers' scoring came from somewhere other than where it was drawn up with a forward who scored, left and came back twice, and a substitute who entered for a defender and beat a ranked opponent's goalkeeper anyway. Rutgers had a third goal chalked off for offside in the 38th and won by two without it. Princeton controlled the final 45 minutes and had nothing to show for it.

Rutgers had needed only the first 40.

description: Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores opted to ease veteran safety Harrison Smith in the Week 1 win over the Green Bay Packers. fullText:
Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores opted to ease veteran safety Harrison Smith in the Week 1 win over the Green Bay Packers. Smith played 26 snaps, with 19 coming in coverage situations against the Packers, leading to a 48.0 PFF defensive grade.

Smith recorded three pressures, one QB hit, two hurries, and one tackle. Meanwhile, in coverage, the veteran safety allowed two receptions for 27 yards. After missing OTAs, training camp, and the preseason, the Green Bay game let Smith start easing back into action.

On Sept. 15, Flores spoke to the media and shared an update on Smith, including whether he intends to ramp up the veteran's snap count in Week 2 against the Chicago Bears.

"We'll take [Smith's snap count] day-to-day as we put together the game plan," Flores told reporters. "We've been through the early-down portion of it, and we'll get into more of the second and long third down this afternoon, this evening.

"As we start to talk about it, that's when a lot of the play time starts to come alive. Who do we want in this spot [and] who do we want in this spot? Who do we want in this spot? How much of this are we doing? So, I really can't answer that right now, but it was a great first week for him."

While opting for a day-by-day approach to determine Smith's snap count and ease him back into NFL action, Flores praised the veteran's ability to go from not being part of OTAs and training camp to playing an NFL game in a little over a week.

"I don't even know if it was 10 days after he signed, something like that, and so, to go in and play, honestly, I don't even know how many snaps he played, but to go in and play in two-minute situations and third downs and make some plays, I thought it was a good showing," Flores added.

"I certainly couldn't go out there and play a game coming off the street; I thought it was great that he looked good, ran pretty well. And as we go, you just assume he'll get in better shape and be ready for more snaps. But we'll take that day-to-day and see where we're at."

The Vikings will need a fresh, ready-to-make-an-impact Smith, given that they'll face a high-powered Bears offense in Week 2. Recently, Flores spoke with the media about the Bears' offense under head coach Ben Johnson, whom Flores has faced often since Johnson served as the Detroit Lions' offensive coordinator.

"I think the first thing is that all 11 guys are involved," Flores told reporters on Sept. 15. "The receivers are blocking, the tight ends, obviously the offensive line, the quarterback's part of it as far as getting the run going in the right direction wherever that happens to be, based on front, shell coverage versus post-safety coverage.

"There's a lot of different variables, and in some systems, it's, 'Hey, we always do this, or we always do that.' In this particular one – it can go, it seems like, based on my interpretation of it and watching it – this could go a few different ways and based on a few different things. So, I think that's part of it."

title: Senate advances the Protect College Sports Act
description: ESPN has gotten its apparent wish.
fullText:
ESPN has gotten its apparent wish. Partially, for now.

The Senate has passed the Protect College Sports Act, by a vote of 74-24. It must now clear the House of Representatives.

The vote comes three days after ESPN put Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas), one of the bill's sponsors, on its flagship college football show to advocate for the passage of the act, without a contemporaneous opposing point of view. And while Stephen A. Smith has apparently chastised me for suggesting that everyone at ESPN supports the Protect College Sports Act, I don't believe that.

It was not my intent to put everyone at ESPN in the same bucket, and I apologize if I created that impression. My point was and is that ESPN's corporate position seems to be that it supports the bill, as evidenced by the fact that two of its most prominent college football analysts (Nick Saban and Pat McAfee) have argued for its passage on GameDay without any real pushback by other panelists, by Disney's reported lobbying for the bill, and by the misguided decision to platform Cruz without offering a voice representing the other side.

Here's a thought — they could have let Smith interview Cruz.

Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) also opposes the Protect College Sports Act. I'll be interviewing him on Thursday morning, for a special edition of #PFTPM.

I'd love to chop it up with Stephen A., too. We agree on plenty of things. On the things we disagree, there's a chance that, through open and honest discourse, we'd better understand each other's points of view. The country currently needs a lot more of that.

The country does not need a federal law that "saves" college sports, in my opinion. College sports are doing just fine, and the system should be required to clean up its own mess without a federal bailout that artificially limits the compensation and freedom of the people who generate the vast majority of the revenue, while leaving unrestricted the ability of coaches to hopscotch the map in chase of their next bag of cash.

The Toronto Raptors, after much ado, have officially brought back Kawhi Leonard in a trade with the Los Angeles Clippers, sending Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two unprotected first-round picks (2031 and 2033), an unprotected pick swap in 2027, and two second-round selections (2030 and 2033). This finally brought an end to a trade saga that faced a long delay amid the NBA's investigation into the Clippers' cap circumvention with Leonard.

Now that the dust has settled, the Raptors can now focus on next season and how Leonard improves the team tenfold. Leonard is a former NBA champion with Toronto, and he is a true game-changer whenever he's out there on the court. Of course, there are always going to be health concerns with Leonard, but he is coming off a season in which he averaged 28/6/4 in 65 games for the Clippers — providing hope that, perhaps, he can sustain a spell of good health moving forward.

It seems as though returning to the Raptors was always meant to be for Leonard. Even Scottie Barnes must have been looking forward to suiting up alongside Leonard for a long time, as he admitted even before he entered the NBA that The Klaw is someone he wants to play with someday. Now, his wish has become a reality.

title: ‘I’m Going To Do A Demolition Job’ – Jonathan Haggerty Out To Silence Hiroki Akimoto On Home Turf At ONE SAMURAI 4
description: "The General" is ready to take out another Japanese star in Tokyo's Ariake Arena on October 17.
fullText:
ONE Bantamweight Kickboxing World Champion Jonathan "The General" Haggerty has hunted this matchup for years. Now that he has finally cornered his target, he fully plans to make an example of him.

The British superstar defends his twenty-six pounds of gold against former divisional king Hiroki Akimoto in the main event of ONE SAMURAI 4 inside the Ariake Arena in Tokyo, Japan, on Saturday, October 17.

This kind of palpable anticipation does not build overnight. "The General" has tracked the Japanese challenger's career for years, long before the two were formally matched up, and few opponents have ever earned this level of profound respect from him.

That respect carries real weight given exactly who it is coming from. Haggerty — aiming for his 25th career victory — does not hand out praise easily, especially heading into a clash where his own World Title is on the line.

"I feel excited now that it's finally here. Me and Akimoto are ready to fight. For years, I've always wanted to fight him. I've considered him probably one of the best in the division.

"He's fought the best. His style as well…I like his style. I feel like our styles will gel well together, and it'll provide a good, explosive fight for the fans."

That mutual respect explains why the 29-year-old has followed his opponent's recent form so closely, particularly the grueling stretch that ultimately earned the Japanese star a coveted shot at regaining the belt that was once in his possession.

After all, Akimoto's arduous path back to this moment was not a straight line. He opened his ONE Championship tenure with an impressive 6-1 stretch before dropping three straight.

Then, he completely turned things around with three impressive decision wins, the last of which came against Taimu Hisai at ONE SAMURAI 1 — the exact same card where Haggerty put on a five-round masterclass against Yuki Yoza to retain his bantamweight kickboxing throne.

"He's been in the organization for a long time. He's fought the best. And now it's his time to challenge me for the belt. He's done what he's had to do.

"He's beaten whoever they've put in front of him. Meanwhile, I've basically beaten the top opponents in the division now, so it was only right for him to get his opportunity."

Competing in enemy territory fundamentally adds an extra layer of adversity to any title defense, and Haggerty knows better than most what awaits him walking into Akimoto's home country.

The Knowlesy Academy and Team Underground pride already faced a hostile Japanese crowd this past April, and the stark parallels between that night and this one are not lost on the reigning king.

Asked how much of an edge the hometown advantage might actually give his opponent, he did not hesitate for a second.

"I think it works as much as it did for Yuki Yoza. Not a lot. I mean, they can't help him when he's in there. It's just him and me.

"Neither of his coaches can help him either. They can give him instructions, but ultimately, it's me and him in the middle of the ring. I've been in the back garden of every fighter. As long as I turn up, meet him in the middle, then that's it."

Respect for his opponent has certainly not stopped Jonathan Haggerty from identifying exactly where he believes the blockbuster fight will be won. After all, the Englishman's confidence stems not just from his natural talent, but from good old-fashioned elbow grease inside the gym.

"The General" has studied Hiroki Akimoto's game intimately. Stylistically, Haggerty sounds fully convinced he already possesses the precise blueprint to shut down anything the Japanese star lays out on the table.

"He's very one-dimensional, but I also think he's got good combinations. And as I said, he's very explosive. He's got good high kicks. But you could have the best game plan in the world. But when I punch you and when I move around you, it's a different story.

"I do believe I'm going to do a demolition job. Some fights I go in there with game plans and stick to it, but this one I really do think I'm going to put a stop to it – a full stop – and make a real big statement."

Should that destructive plan come together seamlessly, the conversation naturally shifts toward what comes next for the bantamweight kickboxing titleholder, and the pride of London has grand designs on returning to form as the undisputed king of Muay Thai.

Haggerty has made it abundantly clear exactly where his sights are set, pointing directly toward reclaiming the bantamweight Muay Thai crown he lost to "The Kicking Machine" Superlek at ONE 168: Denver back in September 2024.

"Defending the belt means a lot to me, you know. It always has. And to keep defending the belt is the main goal for me.

"But I believe after I defend this belt, Yod-IQ [Or Pimolsri] or Rambolek [Chor Ajalaboon] will be next for me."

title: Dancing with the Stars results: Paralympian Ezra Frech tallies second-best score in season premiere
description: Frech is one of three athletes competing in this year's season of "Dancing with the Stars."
fullText:
"Dancing with the Stars" is back, which means the ballroom is filled with a new cast of contestants hoping to win the Mirrorball Trophy.

This season, the cast was expanded, and that forced a two-night premiere. It began on Tuesday with all of the male performers getting the chance to dance, and will culminate on Wednesday night with the female contestants.

Paralympian Ezra Frech was a fan favorite. Frech was born without most of his left leg and the fingers on his left hand. He competed with a prosthetic leg, and his vignette before his dance showed that he would have unusual limitations while dancing.

The Paralympian has walking and running prosthetics. Even during a practice dance in the vignette, a move caused his leg to come loose from his body, and he had to reattach it.

Even with this added challenge, Frech crushed his dance. He and his partner Daniella Karagach performed a tango to Kelly Clarkson's "Since U Been Gone."

THAT WAS THE BEST DANCE OF THE NIGHT SO FAR.

EZRA GAVE ME FULL BODY CHILLS...... DANIELLA THE FERRARI YOU ARE. #DWTS #DancingWithTheStars #DWTS35 #dwts pic.twitter.com/J0dBAFfJ01

The episode began with an announcement that the judges would start with lower scores this season, and early contestants received 4s and 5s across the board. Frech tallied two 7s and a 6 for a combined score of 20 out of a possible 30. It ended up being the second-highest score of the night, trailing only actor Harry Shrum Jr. by one point.

Frech survived the voting of the first episode and will continue in the competition into next week.

The Paralympian is a two-time gold medalist. He took home the gold at the 2024 Paris Paralympic Games in both the 100m T63 and High jump T63 events. Both of his results from these events resulted in world records.

There are two other athletes in the cast this season. The Savannah Bananas' Jackson Olson began the show (scoring a 15/30), and Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn will compete on Wednesday night.

Conner Leavitt was the male contestant eliminated in the season premiere Tuesday night after taking into consideration the fan voting.

title: 49ers RB Kaelon Black earns rare rookie trust after NFL debut
description: Kaelon Black proved in Week 1 he can perform in Kyle Shanahan's offense for the 49ers.
fullText:
San Francisco 49ers rookie running back Kaelon Black has already earned the rare, coveted trust of Kyle Shanahan and running backs coach Bobby Turner, according to The Athletic's Matt Barrows.

Under Shanahan and John Lynch, rookie leeway has historically been practically non-existent. Since 2017, the franchise has drafted seven running backs, but only Elijah Mitchell burst onto the scene with 19 carries in a season opener and remains the lone draft pick to crack 1,000 career yards for the team.

Mid-round selections are frequently phased out or left fighting an uphill battle, but Black appears to be different after his rookie debut.

As backfield mate Christian McCaffrey manages workload and competitors like Isaac Guerendo and Jordan James face hurdles, Black has wasted no time altering the script. Proving his preseason flashes translated directly to the regular-season stage, the rookie debuted with a stellar 65 yards on 14 carries, securing an immediate rotational snap share.

With the coaching staff firmly in his corner, Black is well on his way to proving he is the exception to the rule.

title: Labor accused of throwing creatives ‘under the bus’ with proposal to ease copyright protections for AI giants
description: Compromise revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, meets Albanese...
fullText:
Compromise revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, meets Albanese ministers

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Albanese government is considering giving AI companies access to Australian creatives’ works by default as it pursues a compromise with US tech giants.

The proposals were revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met with Labor ministers and warned that Australia’s copyright laws were preventing the company from training models locally.

The independent senator David Pocock said the compromise would throw protections for creatives and copyright holders “under the bus” in pursuit of datacentre funding.

“It would mean putting AI companies’ interests over everyday Australians, giving AI companies access to all Australians’ content, unless they opt out,” Pocock said on Tuesday.

“The burden should not fall on Australians to defend the rights they already hold over content they create and own and invest in.”

The proposals were contained in a document Pocock described as screenshots of government’s consultation proposals, tabled in the Senate on Tuesday and titled “AI on Australian Terms”.

AI companies have sought to train their models on content and data online but cannot do so using Australian content due to local copyright rules.

The document raises as a key issue the vast number of small individual creators of online content, for which voluntary deals with AI companies “is not realistic/possible”.

It suggests requiring rights holders “digitally protect” their material if they do not want AI models trained on it – a proposal rights holders say is not feasible.

Under one option it proposes, AI companies would gain the right to access and train models on any unprotected online material as long as they made deals with enough businesses.

Under another, AI companies would do deals with creatives’ rights holder organisations that give the access rights even if the content were made by someone who was not a member of the organisation that won the deal. A licence to access one category of material, such as music or text, would be extended to cover the many different small creators within that industry.

Labor’s industry minister, Tim Ayres, had on Monday said the government’s forthcoming AI rules would “in no way” involve a reduction in copyright protection.

The deputy prime minister Richard Marles, said the federal government was “working at a pace” to respond to the issue of copyright, and maintained that the opportunity to work with US tech giants was a “significant moment for the country”.

“The opportunity for Australia economically is enormous in collaborating with frontier companies … and having frontier training occur in Australia,” he told the ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday evening.

“We want to see this opportunity come to the country [but] it needs to come on terms which are in our national interests.”

Marles confirmed that the federal government had spoken with tech companies in San Francisco in the past fortnight on the issue, adding: “I think this can be done.”

Before the revelations on Tuesday afternoon, the Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said the suggestions of a copyright compromise were “abhorrent”.

“Every Australian deserves to get paid for the work that they make and the work that they do,” Hanson-Young said. “A weakening of the copyright laws letting big tech take the work of Australians for free, not have to pay for it, for their own profit.”

Musicians, writers and artists lobbied against weaker copyright laws this year after reports that AI companies were offering $50bn datacentre investments in exchange.

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, is running the government’s consultation with affected organisations.

A spokesperson for Rowland on Tuesday said the government would ensure any future copyright changes delivered “meaningful control and fair compensation”.

OpenAI’s vice-president for global policy, Ann O’Leary, met ministers and officials this week as the company considers investing in Australia.

In an interview with The Australian newspaper about the prospect of training models here, O’Leary said: “Our company isn’t ready to have that conversation if we can’t get through the gating problem of the copyright barriers.”

The newspaper reported the comments as an “ultimatum” that sought to “strong-arm” the government. Marles said the newspaper was “overstating” the comments. OpenAI has asked the paper to correct its headline and article.

Andrew Charlton, the assistant technology minister, told News24 on Tuesday he hadn’t seen any ultimatum and he would reject one if it were issued.

“We want to support Australian artists,” Charlton said. “We want to give them control over their work. We want to make sure they’re compensated, if they choose to have it used.

“We’re not compromising them or trading them off. So if we lose some datacentres over this, so be it.”

title: Using This Under-Pillow Speaker Is Way More Comfortable Than Sleeping With Earbuds
description: Never again will I lose my AirPods in the sheets.
fullText:
If you're one of those people who can't fall asleep without a "Sleep With Me" podcast droning on, or playing one of those Spotify "Sleep Music 528 Hz" playlists, this week's upgrade is for you. I need my audio to fall asleep, and I usually resort to sleeping in earbuds, but if you're a side sleeper, it can feel like they dig straight into your skull the second you roll over. And just playing audio from your phone speaker is a non-starter when you share the bed with a partner.

The Jabees Peace Duo sleep speaker is one of my favorite solutions to one of my toughest problems: How do you listen to something all night, comfortably, privately, without wearing anything on or in your ears?

The Peace Duo uses my favorite audio trend, bone conduction technology (pillow conduction technology?). Typically, bone conduction devices send sound vibrations directly toward your inner ear, through the bones of your skull, instead of blasting it out through the open air or directly into your ear canals.

This speaker sits under your pillow rather than in or on your body, which is really the whole point of the "private under-pillow listening" claims. The sound stays close to your head and doesn't broadcast across the room the way a phone or bedside speaker would. Paired with a dual-speaker design, it gives you separate left and right listening units, so you get a bit of stereo positioning depending on how you're lying. Plus, it has a reliable 10-hour battery life, so you can run your sleep soundtrack all night without having to think about it.

Before I give my full-fledged endorsement, however, there are a few caveats worth noting. Here's what to actually expect:

There is some sound leakage. If someone's sleeping next to you, they may catch a bit of audio—but it'll be significantly quieter than if you just played the same thing off your phone speaker.

Sound gets muffled coming through the pillow. When using it for spoken-word audio like sleep podcasts, dialogue does lose some clarity—if you need crisp, easily parsed speech, this isn't going to sound like a podcast studio. And it should go without saying that your music won't sound nearly as crisp as it would through earbuds either.

My main reason for this upgrade is wanting a dedicated device I could trust falling asleep with—or else I'd be too paranoid about rolling over on my phone, losing my earbuds in my sheets, or otherwise risking my expensive electronics. It's one less thing to worry about breaking or losing overnight, and for me, it's the most comfortable solution to this specific use case.

And honestly? That slightly muffled quality isn't always a downside! There's something about the softened, pillow-filtered sound that leans into the whole point of falling asleep in the first place. I feel like I'm truly drifting into the sounds, turning my guided meditations into a pleasant, immersive dreamscape.

If you fall asleep to audio every night and you're tired of earbuds falling out or hurting your ears, the Jabees Peace Duo sleep speaker is a comfortable, private way to listen—as long as you're okay trading a little audio quality for a lot more comfort.

title: Why People Are Taping Fitbits to Their Arms
description: I tried this trend, and I have thoughts.
fullText:
The beauty of a smart band is that it isn’t a watch and doesn’t need to act like one. That includes where you wear it: Whoop has the right idea with their bicep band and “any-wear” clothing. Since Google hasn’t released a bicep band for the Fitbit Air, some users are taking matters into their own hands—with rolls of tape.

I’ve watched this trend unfold on the Fitbit Air subreddit, as one person after another realizes they can just tape the device to their arm, or anywhere they want. I’ve actually done something like this before—years ago, I found myself trying to fit the Whoop onto my ankle, and then thought, wait a sec, can’t I just tape it to the side of my leg? (I did, and it worked.)

Taping your Fitbit Air to your arm (without the strap, of course) gets it off your wrist. It means the device is no longer in the way of wrist wraps or kettlebells, and you can wear any kind of sleeves or accessories you like without the Fitbit getting in the way or cramping your style.  These are minor problems, to be sure. But sometimes, it’s nice to just forget you’re wearing something.

People are experimenting with different types of adhesives. One of the more popular is KT tape, the stuff that athletes often use to stabilize a body part that’s giving them some minor trouble. You can also use athletic or medical tape. But I don’t really trust any of those. I find that KT tape can start peeling off in just a day if you do a really sweaty workout and then take a shower. Maybe it’s not supposed to, but it can. Longer strips of tape have plenty of adhesive to keep them on, but a small piece—the size you’d need for a Fitbit—is going to have a harder time doing its job.

The best adhesive for the job is probably a CGM overpatch. CGMs, or continuous glucose monitors, are small plastic devices that are typically stuck on the back of the upper arm. A filament pierces the skin to take readings, but to keep it safely in place, the device itself has an adhesive. You can add some security by applying a large sticker called an overpatch.

These overpatches are perfect for securing a Fitbit to your arm for long-term use. A typical CGM lasts about two weeks, and the Fitbit Air’s battery lasts about a week. If you want the device to stay on through workouts and showers, an overpatch is more than qualified to do the job.

While I’ve taped devices to my body before, I decided to do a proper experiment with the Fitbit Air. I applied it to the back of my arm with an overpatch (similar to this one) and went out for a run. It stuck well despite the sweat, and captured heart rate data that matched well with other devices I used for comparison.

One risk of taping a Fitbit to your body is that not all areas of the body will capture heart rate equally well. The upper arm may not have great access to blood vessels on everyone’s body (we’re all different), but, on the bright side, sticking it under a patch will keep it snug against your skin and block out ambient light. Those factors tend to improve accuracy.

Activity detection may suffer, though. The Fitbit is judging your movement based on what it expects to see your wrist doing in a workout. Your upper arm won’t show the same movements as your wrist, so auto-detection might not work properly. When I took the taped Fitbit out on the road, it didn’t auto-detect my jog. On a second run, I started the workout manually and things went better from there.

Overall, I don’t think taping your Fitbit to your arm is a bad idea. It does have some downsides, though. Auto-detection of workouts might not work as well, and heart rate accuracy will probably depend on the exact location (and how well it performs may vary from person to person).

There’s one other thing I’m dreading, and that’s what happens when I take it off. An overpatch often has adhesive so strong it’s hard to remove at the end of the two-week life of a CGM. If my Fitbit’s battery dies after just a week, I’ll have to peel off the overpatch at that point to charge it, perhaps painfully and with great difficulty. (Pro tip: Remove things like this in the shower; the warm water helps a lot.)

It would also get expensive to apply patches every week, but perhaps that’s worth it if you really don’t like a wristband or if you just want to do this for a specific occasion. About the best I can say is that it’s not a terrible idea.

title: NI squad only picked on merit - O'Neill
description: Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill says he would never take Fifa eligibility rules into consideration when selecting his squad.
fullText:
Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill has said he would never take Fifa eligibility rules into consideration when selecting his squad.

Reaching four senior caps for a country rules out a future switch of international allegiance with the regulations again in the spotlight with regards to Arsenal teenager Ceadach O'Neill.

The 18-year-old won his first two Northern Ireland caps in June friendlies against Guinea and France, and is in the squad for an upcoming Nations League quadruple-header, but has also been subject to an approach from the Republic of Ireland.

After stating that he does not feel it is fair to ask teenagers to make "irreversible" decisions on their international future, Michael O'Neill said he would not consider bringing players into the squad with a view to tying them to Northern Ireland before other associations show interest.

"I wouldn't just put a player on the pitch for that because that would be unfair on the player and I've never done that," he said.

"I've never put a player on the pitch from that point of view. I've always tried to be fair across the board if players deserve the opportunity to play, which Ceadach did.

"Because he trained so well, he got the opportunity to play."

Northern Ireland's latest Nations League campaign starts away to Georgia on 25 September and Ceadach O'Neill is one of four teenagers in the squad alongside Blackburn Rovers defender Tom Atcheson, Everton forward Braiden Graham and Kieran Morrison - the Liverpool winger currently on loan at Sheffield Wednesday.

Atcheson and Morrison were both born in England but qualify for Northern Ireland through grandparents and represented the side at underage level before making their senior bows in March and June respectively.

"Kieran deserved the chance to play because he'd been around the Liverpool first team. He'd been showing up well in training as well, both in March and June," said O'Neill after naming a 28-man squad for the four-game window.

"Braiden is the same. They're there because this is the next step for them. I believe being part of the senior international squad will help them, will help their club careers, but they merit a place in a 28-man squad. They merit their place in that squad over some players that aren't in my opinion.

"My job is to protect the national team going forward and to build the squad as strong as possible. To do that you have to look at your young players."

Entrusting young players with key roles, in many cases before they are established at their club sides, has been common practice for Northern Ireland in recent years.

Conor Bradley, Isaac Price and the Charles brothers, Shea and Pierce, all made their international debuts as teenagers, while Sunderland pair Dan Ballard and Trai Hume broke into the side as 20-year-olds.

O'Neill himself won his first cap at 18 in 1988 and cited Norman Whiteside making an international debut as a 17-year-old at the 1982 World Cup as another example of how the side relied on early exposure for young players long before any eligibility issues came to the fore.

"This is not new for Northern Ireland. We've done this in the past," he added.

"I understand how this works. We're doing it based on the level of the player and that's the most important thing."

title: Messi in Argentina squad for farewell friendly
description: Argentina name Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.
fullText:
Argentina have named Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.

Messi announced his retirement from Argentina duty in August in the wake of his country's defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final and after saying he was considering his future in football following the death of his father, Jorge.

The 39-year-old, who captained Argentina when they won the 2022 World Cup, said the decision to stop playing for La Albiceleste hurt him "deeply" but that he had "given it my all" and had "nothing left to give".

Messi, an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner who currently plays for Inter Miami, is Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player, having scored 125 goals in 207 appearances.

"We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on 6 October here in Argentina," said Argentine FA president Claudio Tapia.

River Plate's Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which has an 85,000 capacity, will host the game against Benin.

Argentina's 2022 World Cup winners have also been invited to the match, which Tapia said would be an "unforgettable" occasion.

Messi retires from Argentina duty with 'nothing left to give'

Messi unsure he will play 'much longer' after father's death

Argentina were ordered to play their next two home matches with 50% capacity, although one match of that sanction was suspended, for breaches of the Fifa disciplinary code during the World Cup.

The punishment related to using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, team misconduct, and discriminatory chants and gestures by its supporters.

After defeating England 2-1 in the World Cup semi-final, several Argentina players held up a banner claiming Argentine sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory.

As they play friendlies against Bolivia on 30 September in Cordoba and Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires on 3 October, it should mean the punishment will have been served before the Benin game.

Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes and team-mate Nahuel Molina are not expected to be available as they were given respective 10-game and seven-match suspensions for their part in on-field clashes following their country's defeat by Spain in the World Cup final.

title: Let them ref the games and be humans - Andrews
description: After Brentford overcame Reading to reach the Carabao Cup fourth round, head coach Keith Andrews believes the video assistant referee (VAR) is preventing referees from making decisions in matches.
fullText:
Brentford head coach Keith Andrews believes the video assistant referee (VAR) is preventing referees from making decisions in matches.

As his Bees progressed to the Carabao Cup fourth round with a battling 2-1 win at League One side Reading, Andrews said he was not happy with the officiating.

Reading defender Paudie O'Connor had a goal for a first-half overhead kick ruled out by referee Tom Nield for a high boot, prompting Royals boss Leam Richardson to say it was "possibly in the top three [wrong] decisions that I've seen in my career - and I've seen thousands of games and played in hundreds".

With no VAR used at this stage of the EFL Cup, Andrews added: "It's been a tough week for officials as everybody is probably aware.

"I think we just need to let them ref the game and be human beings and make decisions.

"We have gone through a period in the game where I feel like they weren't actually making decisions in both boxes because of the technology we have in the game and I feel like that is a real shame."

His comments followed the admission of Pro Ref to an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's winning goal for Manchester City in their Premier League encounter at Manchester United on Sunday.

There was intense debate over whether the goal should have been disallowed for City midfielder Enzo Fernandez - who was in an offside position - interfering with play as he dived, attempting to head the ball in a central position before Haaland's finish.

Andrews, whose Brentford side are seventh in the Premier League, said referees were no longer allowed to "make mistakes".

"I always felt as a player, when there was a relationship with an official that was built on respect and being able to speak to each other in a certain way," he added.

"We've gone away from allowing them to officiate and allowing them to make mistakes and I think it is a real shame.

"Now they are having to go back to that and it's not the habits they have had in recent years."

On Sunday's refereeing error in the Manchester derby, Andrews said it was "pretty alarming" Haaland's goal was allowed to stand.

"The first thing was whether [Erling] Haaland was offside and then obviously [Enzo] Fernandez was. It's a shame," he admitted.

Nearly 2 years after Helene, remains of missing Tennessee woman found
description: Human remains found in Tennessee nearly two years after Hurricane Helene have been identified as Nancy Tucker, who went missing in the storm.
fullText:
Nearly two years after Hurricane Helene devastated parts of the Southeast, authorities have identified the remains of a Tennessee woman who had been missing since the storm.

Medical examiners confirmed the remains found Sept. 12, in the Jackson Island area of the Nolichucky River are those of Nancy Tucker, according to the Washington County Sheriff's Office.

Tucker was the last person reported missing in Washington County, about 65 miles north of Asheville, North Carolina, and 90 miles northeast of Knoxville, Tennessee, following the catastrophic flooding caused by Helene.

Her remains were found by debris removal specialists working in the area. The remains were taken to the William Jenkins Forensics Center at East Tennessee State University for examination and identification, according to AccuWeather.

Tucker and her husband, Jimmy, lived about four and a half miles upstream from Jackson Island. Jimmy Tucker's body was recovered days after Helene struck the region.

The discovery comes as cleanup crews continue to work through debris left behind by the storm, which made landfall in Florida's Big Bend region as a Category 4 hurricane on Sept. 26, 2024, before moving inland across the Southeast.

Torrential rain caused catastrophic flooding across the southern Appalachians, with some of the worst damage occurring in western North Carolina and eastern Tennessee.

Helene was responsible for at least 250 deaths in the United States, according to the National Hurricane Center.

In a February 2026 report, the National Hurricane Center said Helene was the deadliest hurricane in the contiguous United States since Hurricane Katrina in 2005. At least 175 of the deaths were directly caused by the storm, including people killed by freshwater flooding, storm surge, wind, tornadoes and other direct effects.

Tennessee recorded 18 deaths connected to Helene, according to the National Hurricane Center. The flooding was particularly deadly in East Tennessee, where swollen rivers and streams overwhelmed communities.

The number of people still missing remains less certain.

The National Hurricane Center's latest update to its Helene report, published Feb. 17, 2026, said at least five people remained missing in western North Carolina and eastern Tennessee.

With Tucker now identified, at least four people could remain missing, although authorities have not announced an updated regional total.

Hurricane Helene made landfall in Florida as a Category 4 hurricane, but some of its most destructive impacts occurred hundreds of miles inland across the southern Appalachians.

Helene carried an enormous amount of tropical moisture as it moved north. When the storm reached the mountains, the terrain forced the moist air upward, producing heavy rainfall over an area that had already received rain before Helene arrived.

The mountainous terrain also caused water to rush rapidly downhill into creeks and rivers. That combination of extreme rainfall, saturated ground and steep slopes led to catastrophic flooding and landslides across western North Carolina and eastern Tennessee.

title: Trump’s tariffs slashed jobs and wage growth. Now companies are funneling their chunk of the $100 billion in refunds to supplement workers’ retirement
description: Williams Sonoma and TJX plan to give millions of dollars in tariff refunds back to employees through 401(k) payments and bonuses.
fullText:
In March, shortly after the Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump's International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) tariffs and paved the way for $100 billion in import taxes being redistributed back to American importers, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer shared his idea of what these companies should do with this influx of cash.

"If I were these companies, and somehow they get this windfall, the most important thing and the smartest thing they should do is give it as bonuses to their workers," Greer told CNBC.

It appears some companies have heeded Greer's suggestion. As businesses receive more than $100 billion the U.S. Treasury has doled out in refunds since May, many are vowing to lower prices or pay down debts. A handful, however, are giving the cash back to their employees.

In its second quarter earnings report last month, houseware brand Williams Sonoma said it would allocate $10 million for one-time payments to 401(k) accounts to eligible employees  "in recognition of their efforts navigating the IEEPA tariffs."

"We're so appreciative to have the money back and to be able to reward our employees with part of it," President and CEO Laura Alber said on an earnings call. "They have done such an amazing job."

TJX, which received $331 million total in tariff refunds, will similarly put a portion of its aggregated refunds into paying employees extra.

"Due to these tariff refunds, the company accrued incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible associates globally," a spokesperson told Fortune in a statement.

American companies and consumers alike have kept a close eye on the tariff refund process, particularly after Federal Reserve research showed they were the ones shouldering the brunt of the tariff costs. While companies like Walmart and FedEx have promised to compensate consumers for tariff-related inflation through lower prices or direct rebates, the unconventional decision to hand employees cash from tariff refunds indicates just what a pervasive impact the import taxes had on U.S. companies.

"Companies have a lot of different margins for how they adjust to tariffs," Alex Durante, senior economist at the Tax Foundation, told Fortune. "They could pass all of it along to consumers, they could also reduce investment, they could reduce hiring, they could cut back on certain employer perks and forms of compensation, if they wish. And I think that this is just perhaps another way of thinking about that."

title: Italy extends border controls on visitors from Spain as migration feud continues
description: Italy on Tuesday extended for another 15 days border checks on visitors from Spain that it imposed after more than 72,000 migrants poured into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta from Morocco in ...
fullText:
ROME (AP) — Italy on Tuesday extended for another 15 days border checks on visitors from Spain that it imposed after more than 72,000 migrants poured into Spain's North African territory of Ceuta from Morocco in late July.

Spain, which had responded to Rome's sanctions with its own border checks on people coming from Italy, also extended its tit-for-tat measures for another 15 days, the Spanish foreign ministry said.

Although most of the migrants returned to Morocco, the government of Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni and other hawkish European leaders used the chaos in Ceuta in July to criticize the migration policies of Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. Months before the Ceuta crisis, his government had carried out a migrant legalization push.

Italy imposed the border controls – which amounted to random police checks at airports and seaports for passengers arriving from Spain – by claiming a threat to its internal security.

The Italian Interior Ministry used that same threat to justify extending the border checks Tuesday. In a statement it said it had informed the European Union and other European governments that "high risks to internal security persist, in addition to a potential threat related to possible terrorist infiltration."

Spain, for its part, said it too was extending the retaliatory measures since the conditions that led to them – Italy's original sanctions – remained in place.

The 27-member EU bloc has a visa-free travel area known as Schengen that allows citizens of most EU countries to travel easily across borders for work and pleasure.

According to the EU, member states are allowed to temporarily reintroduce controls at the EU's so-called internal borders in case of a serious threat, such as one to internal security. But it also says border controls should be applied as a last resort in exceptional situations, and must be time-limited.

Even before Italy imposed the border checks, travelers leaving Ceuta and Melilla, Spain's other territory in North Africa, were already subject to EU border checks at ports and airports.

NGOs reported that more than 140 people died in the attempt to cross into the territory, including some who drowned or were trampled in a stampede to cross a breakwater barrier.

More than 5,000 migrants have remained in Ceuta, prolonging a humanitarian crisis that has become a political liability for Sánchez in Spain and beyond. His government had decided to carry out an amnesty for immigrants without residency permits who could prove they had been living in the country for at least five months and arrived before Jan. 1 this year. Over 1 million people applied before the window closed.

title: High-profile Democrat breaks with party, embraces key pieces of Trump agenda
description: Haley Stevens backs Trump administration policies on critical minerals, data centers and public equity stakes in high-growth industries like Intel.
fullText:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN — Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., threw her support behind three of the Trump administration's signature economic policies in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Collaboration between ratepayers and data center developers, public stakes in high-growth industries and loan guarantees for critical mineral extraction are all areas where the Michigan congresswoman says the Trump administration is charting the right course. She also pointed to bolstering American manufacturing and deterring the nation's adversaries from hostage taking as areas where she believes bipartisan collaboration is possible.

"It's not just about taxation," Stevens told Fox News Digital when asked how revenues can be raised to fund healthcare and infrastructure programs. "If federal dollars are used, like what Mr. Elon Musk got from the federal government, so potentially this current administration could be right that ownership stakes should be on the table."

Progressive Praise For Trump As Warren Backs Push To Curb Defense Contractor Ceo Payouts

The Trump administration has increasingly pursued direct equity stakes, alongside grants and loans, to steer capital into industries it considers strategically important, such as semiconductors and critical minerals.

For instance, the administration converted $8.9 billion in federal funding into a 9.9% nonvoting stake in Intel, while the Pentagon took a 15% stake in rare-earth producer MP Materials. Both investments have increased in value since the government took them, although those gains are not realized until the shares are sold.

While Stevens thinks stimulating economic growth is part of the equation for balancing the federal balance sheet, she did say that the "wealthiest of the wealthy" should "absolutely" pay 

Stevens rose to national prominence during her primary contest against Abdul El-Sayed, who has since become the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan. She cast herself as a more moderate alternative to El-Sayed, who she accused of unfairly singling out Jewish Americans.

Democrats' Civil War Heads To Michigan Where Progressives Face Biggest Test Yet In High-stakes Senate Showdown

Though the primary feud between the two was intense, Stevens endorsed El-Sayed following a narrow primary defeat and signaled that, while she may agree with President Donald Trump on some things, she still sees his broader agenda as dangerous for America.

"I personally think [Republican nominee] Mike Rogers is going to continue to rubber-stamp Donald Trump's chaotic agenda," she said in an interview after endorsing El-Sayed. "People are going to make a personal and private decision. I am not on the ballot in Michigan."

Likewise, the White House isn't particularly warm towards Stevens.

"It's rich that Haley Stevens claims to support President Trump's proven economic agenda after voting against the President over 80 percent of the time in Congress – including on the Great One Big Beautiful Bill, which is the largest working-class tax cut in history," White House spokesman Kush Desai told Fox News Digital.

Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens Backs El-sayed After Narrow Primary Defeat, Calls Socialism 'Dangerous'

Though Stevens is a loyal Democrat, she says that doesn't prevent her from working across the aisle, especially on local issues.

For that reason, she threw her support behind the Trump administration's Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a collaborative framework bringing together utilities, data center developers, cooperatives and state governments to keep energy prices down amidst the massive buildout of AI infrastructure.

"I think collaboration is always a promising first step and path forward," Stevens told Fox News Digital when asked about the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. "Before I was in Congress, I had also worked on the bipartisan auto-rescue task force in the Obama administration. I was an Obama appointee, but there were also Bush appointees who stayed on, and there frankly were Republicans who were on the task force. And the reason I'm mentioning the auto task force is that we coordinated at the local level. We coordinated large-scale federal resources."

Later in the interview, Stevens stressed to Fox News Digital that she is "really fired up about critical minerals," arguing that America makes itself vulnerable to China by failing to increase domestic production. She listed loan guarantees for mining firms, a policy currently being carried out by the Trump administration, as something she supports.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

Looking forward, Stevens — who has a strong record of bipartisan work — highlighted a few areas she believes are fertile ground for Republicans and Democrats to work together.

"[Rep.] French Hill, who's a Republican from Arkansas and a great congressman, French Hill and I have passed considerable pieces of legislation to stand up to America's enemies, to stand up to our detractors, and that continues to be an area where I believe that we will see more bipartisan collaboration," she told Fox News Digital. "I also feel very strongly and I'm very proud to serve as the bipartisan caucus chair of the manufacturing caucus, our industrial sector, and one of the areas of great success for me in the Congress was, as a midwesterner, working with colleagues on the other side of the aisle to grow our manufacturing economy."

title: Two House Democrats defect again on key vote for Trump agenda
description: House Democrats are fuming after a pair of centrist members once again defied their party leaders by voting to help advance a key White House priority — the second time in recent weeks.
fullText:
House Democrats are fuming after a pair of centrist members once again defied their party leaders by voting to help advance a key White House priority — the second time in recent weeks.

The frustrations at those two Democrats — in particular, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who is seeking reelection in a battleground seat — are so high that they led to a confrontation on the House floor Tuesday evening between the Washington congresswoman and a top party leader, according to a person familiar with the exchange.

Rep. Katherine Clark, the No. 2 House Democrat and party whip, appeared to raise her voice in an intense conversation on the floor with Gluesenkamp Perez shortly after the vote, that person said. (The other Democratic defector, Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, is retiring after his term and has faced less party blowback.)

The vote the two Democrats defected on is known as a rule vote. Typically, members of the minority party stick together to oppose these kind of procedural votes, which the majority party needs to bring bills to the floor.

Democrats are particularly irate given that one of the bills that can now be brought to the floor is a Russian sanctions bill that President Donald Trump himself has championed. The White House has made it such a high priority that some in the administration privately reached out to at least one House Democratic centrist, attempting to convince that member to support the GOP procedural vote in exchange for a community project back home, that member told CNN. That member ultimately opposed the GOP procedural vote.

While some Democrats support the Russia sanctions bill, they said they were not willing to back a GOP rule — and cross party leadership — to get that result.

"I'm proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America — people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism," Gluesenkamp Perez said on X, adding, "My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fueling this war."

The decision by the two Democrats to once again flout their leadership has quickly resurfaced a complicated debate about party discipline within the caucus. Democrats had already been discussing ways to punish members who oppose the party on key procedural votes after the last episode. Now, in the final week of session before the midterms, those conversations are quickly heating up.

Another top Democrat, Rep. Pete Aguilar, later called out the two defectors and said their caucus would discuss potential punishments for the members.

Asked about enforcing party discipline, he said, "We'll have some conversations as a family, and we'll go from there."

And he issued a terse warning to fellow Democrats about the behavior: "That's not what we should be doing."
